candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 13:8 (Abraham cycle (13:8)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And he built there an altar, and he offered thereon a burnt-offering to the Lord who had appeared unto him, and he called upon the name of the Lord' — at Bethel, prior to all Mosaic legislation, Abram constitutes the first patriarchal altar. The Tewahedo Liturgy of Abraham (Anaphora of the Patriarchs, used in periodic monastic-festal commemoration) draws its canonical warrant from this verse: legitimate altar precedes Mosaic priestly ordination by centuries, anchoring the Tewahedo conviction that the Christian altar is patriarchal-prototypical, not merely a Mosaic-replacement.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Abram returned to the place where he had at the first made the altar, and he called there on the name of the Lord, and said: Thou art my God, the Eternal God' — after the Egypt-sojourn (13:11-15), Abram returns to the Bethel altar. Jubilees inscribes return-to-altar as the canonical post-failure rhythm. Tewahedo confession-practice (näsḫa) draws on this pattern: the penitent returns precisely to the same altar previously profaned, not to a substitute. The Andǝmta names this 'Abram's return' (mätsä Abram) as the type of restoration after Diaspora exile.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 13:25 (Abraham cycle (13:25)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the fourteenth year of this jubilee, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tergal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Sellasar, made war against Bera king of Sodom and against Birsha king of Gomorrah... And Abram numbered three hundred and eighteen of his trained men born in his house, and he pursued after them as far as Dan, and routed them by night' — the Genesis-14 Melchizedek narrative is preserved with the tithe-paid detail (13:25-27 in Charles). Jubilees uniquely emphasizes that the tithe was paid out of the rescued Lot's-property spoils and confirmed in heavenly tablets — making it the canonical first-tithe before Mosaic tithing law. Tewahedo monastic ǝʾǝsär (tithe) collection appeals to this passage as the priestly-pre-Mosaic warrant for tithing on agrarian + military goods alike.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Abram returned to the place where he had at the first made the altar, and he called there on the name of the Lord, and said: Thou art my God, the Eternal God' — after the Egypt-sojourn (13:11-15), Abram returns to the Bethel altar. Jubilees inscribes return-to-altar as the canonical post-failure rhythm. Tewahedo confession-practice (näsḫa) draws on this pattern: the penitent returns precisely to the same altar previously profaned, not to a substitute. The Andǝmta names this 'Abram's return' (mätsä Abram) as the type of restoration after Diaspora exile.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the fourteenth year of this jubilee, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tergal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Sellasar, made war against Bera king of Sodom and against Birsha king of Gomorrah... And Abram numbered three hundred and eighteen of his trained men born in his house, and he pursued after them as far as Dan, and routed them by night' — the Genesis-14 Melchizedek narrative is preserved with the tithe-paid detail (13:25-27 in Charles). Jubilees uniquely emphasizes that the tithe was paid out of the rescued Lot's-property spoils and confirmed in heavenly tablets — making it the canonical first-tithe before Mosaic tithing law. Tewahedo monastic ǝʾǝsär (tithe) collection appeals to this passage as the priestly-pre-Mosaic warrant for tithing on agrarian + military goods alike.

'And he built there an altar, and he offered thereon a burnt-offering to the Lord who had appeared unto him, and he called upon the name of the Lord' — at Bethel, prior to all Mosaic legislation, Abram constitutes the first patriarchal altar. 'And Abram returned to the place where he had at the first made the altar, and he called there on the name of the Lord, and said: Thou art my God, the Eternal God' — after the Egypt-sojourn (13:11-15), Abram returns to the Bethel altar. Jubilees inscribes return-to-altar as the canonical post-failure rhythm. Tewahedo confession-practice (näsḫa) draws on this pattern: the penitent returns precisely to the same altar previously profaned, not to a substitute. The Andǝmta names this 'Abram's return' (mätsä Abram) as the type of restoration after Diaspora exile.
